'''''Arundo donax''''' is a tall [[Perennial plant|perennial]] [[cane (grass)|cane]]. It is one of several so-called [[Reed (plant)|reed]] species. It has several common names including '''giant cane''', '''elephant grass''', '''carrizo''', '''arundo''', '''Spanish cane''', '''Colorado river reed''', '''wild cane''', and '''giant reed'''. ''Arundo'' and ''donax'' are respectively the old Latin and Greek names for reed.<ref>Gledhill D. 1985. ''The Names of Plants''. Cambridge University Press. {{ISBN | 978-0-5213-6675-5}}</ref>

''Arundo donax'' grows in damp soils, either fresh or moderately saline, and is native to the [[Greater Middle East]].<ref name=CABI>CABI, 2020. Arundo donax (giant reed). In: Invasive Species Compendium. Wallingford, UK: CAB International. https://www.cabi.org/isc/datasheet/1940</ref><ref name=GISD>Global Invasive Species Database (2020) Species profile: Arundo donax. Downloaded from http://www.iucngisd.org/gisd/species.php?sc=112 on 12-01-2020.</ref> It has been widely planted and naturalised in the mild temperate, subtropical and tropical regions of both hemispheres, especially in the [[Mediterranean Basin|Mediterranean]], [[California]], the western [[Pacific]] and the [[Caribbean]] and is considered invasive in North America and Oceania.<ref name="doi.org">Perdue, R.E. Arundo donax—Source of musical reeds and industrial cellulose. Econ Bot 12, 368–404 (1958). https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02860024</ref><ref name=CABI /><ref name=GISD /><ref>{{cite web | title=Catalogue of Life 2008 | url=http://www.catalogueoflife.org/show_species_details.php?record_id=726103}}</ref><ref name=":0">Lambert, A.M., Dudley, T.L. and Saltonstall, K., 2010. Ecology and impacts of the large-statured invasive grasses Arundo donax and Phragmites australis in North America. Invasive Plant Science and Management, 3(4), pp. 489–494.</ref> It forms dense stands on disturbed sites, sand dunes, in wetlands and [[riparian]] habitats.
[[Image:Illustration Arundo donax0.jpg|thumb|upright|''Arundo donax'']]

==Description==
''Arundo donax'' generally grows to {{convert|6|m|ft}} in height, or in ideal conditions can exceed {{convert|10|m|ft}}. The hollow stems are {{convert|2|to|3|cm|in}} in diameter. The grey-green swordlike [[leaf|leaves]] are alternate, {{convert|30|to|60|cm|in}} long and {{convert|2|to|6|cm|in}} wide with a tapered tip, and have a hairy tuft at the base. Overall, the plant resembles an outsize common reed (''[[Phragmites australis]]'') or a [[bamboo]] (subfamily Bambusoideae).{{cn|date=November 2024}}

''A. donax'' [[flower]]s in late summer, bearing upright, feathery plumes {{convert|40|to|60|cm|in}} long, that are usually seedless or with seeds that are rarely fertile.<ref>(Johnson et al. 2006)</ref> Instead, it mostly reproduces vegetatively by tough, fibrous underground [[rhizome]]s that form knotty, spreading mats which penetrate deep into the soil, up to {{convert|1|m|ft}} deep.<ref name=":1">{{Cite book |last=Harrington |first=C. 1 |url=https://www.cal-ipc.org/docs/ip/management/wwh/pdf/18601.pdf |title=The Weed Workers' Handbook |last2=Hayes |first2=A. |publisher=The Watershed Project: [[California Invasive Plant Council]] |year=2004 |location=Richmond, CA}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |first=Peter |last=Alden |url=http://worldcat.org/oclc/37696259 |title=National Audubon Society field guide to the Pacific Northwest |date=1998 |publisher= [[Knopf Publishing]] |isbn=0-679-44679-6 |oclc=37696259}}</ref> Stem and rhizome pieces less than {{convert|5|cm|in}} long and containing a single [[Node (botany)|node]] could sprout readily under a variety of conditions.<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal |last=Boose |last2=Holt |date=April 1999 |title=Environmental effects on asexual reproduction in''Arundo donax'' |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1046/j.1365-3180.1999.00129.x |journal= [[Weed Research]] |volume=39 |issue=2 |pages=117–127 |doi=10.1046/j.1365-3180.1999.00129.x |issn=0043-1737|url-access=subscription }}</ref> This [[vegetative propagation]] appears well adapted to floods, which may break up individual ''A. donax'' clumps, spreading the pieces, which may sprout and colonise downstream.<ref name=":1" />

==Biology==
''Arundo donax'' is a tall, perennial grass in the subfamily [[Arundinoideae]], characterised by [[C3 photosynthesis]]. The [[plant stem|stems]] produced during the first growing season are unbranched and photosynthetic. In the [[Mediterranean]], where a temperate climate is characterized by warm and dry summer and mild winter, new shoots of giant reed emerge around March, growing rapidly in June and July and producing stems and leaves. From late July the lower leaves start to dry, depending on seasonal temperature patterns. Drying accelerates during autumn when [[anthesis]] occurs from the beginning of October to the end of November. In this [[phenological]] stage moisture content falls significantly. In the low temperatures of winter giant reed stops its growth; regrowth occurs in springtime. Giant reed behaves as an annual in [[Central Europe]] where soil temperatures are low, due to poor freeze tolerance of the [[rhizomes]].

The base growth temperature reported for giant reed is {{cvt|7|C}},<ref>Spencer, D.F., Ksander, G.G., 2006. Estimate ''Arundo donax'' ramet recruitment using [[degree-day]] based equation. Aquat. Bot. 85, 282–288.</ref> with a maximum temperature of {{cvt|30|C}}. It has a high [[photosynthetic capacity]], associated with absence of light saturation. [[Carbon dioxide]] exchange rates are high compared to other [[C3 carbon fixation|{{c3}}]] and [[C4 carbon fixation|{{c4}}]] species; maximum CO<sub>2</sub> uptake ranged from 19.8 to 36.7 μmol/s·m<sup>2</sup> under natural conditions, depending on [[irradiance]] and leaf age. Carbon dioxide exchange is regulated by leaf conductance.<ref>Rossa B, TuAers AV, Naidoo G, von Willert DJ. 1998. ''Arundo donax'' L. (Poaceae)—a C<sub>3</sub> species with unusually high photosynthetic capacity. Botanica Acta. 111:216–21.</ref>

Studies have found this plant to be rich in active [[tryptamine]] compounds, but there are more indications of the plants in [[India]] having these compounds than in the [[United States]].<ref name="erowid1">[http://www.erowid.org/plants/arundo_donax/arundo_donax_info1.shtml Erowid ''Arundo Donax'' Info Page 1]</ref> [[Toxins]] such as [[bufotenidine]]<ref name="erowid3">[http://www.erowid.org/plants/arundo_donax/arundo_donax_info3.shtml#plentiful Erowid ''Arundo Donax'' Info Page 3]</ref> and [[gramine]]<ref name="erowid1" /> have also been found.

The dried rhizome with the stem removed has been found to contain 0.0057% [[dimethyltryptamine|DMT]], 0.026% [[bufotenine]], 0.0023% 5-MeO-MMT.<ref name="erowid1" /> The flowers are also known to have DMT and the 5-methoxylated N-demethylated analogue, also [[5-MeO-NMT]]. The quite toxic quaternary methylated salt of DMT, bufotenidine,<ref name="erowid1" /> has been found in the flowers, and the cyclic [[dehydrobufotenidine]] has been found in the roots.{{Citation needed|date=August 2010}}
''A. donax'' is also known to release [[volatile organic compounds]] (VOCs), mainly [[isoprene]].<ref>Owen, S.M., Boissard, C., and Hewitt, C. N. Atmospheric Environment, 35, 2001, pp 5393–5409</ref>

==Genetic background==
In most areas where giant reed grows ([[Mediterranean area]] and [[United States|US]]), viable [[seeds]] are not produced.<ref>Saltonstall, K., Lambert, A., Meyerson, L.A., 2010. Genetics and reproduction of common (''Phragmites australis'') and giant reed (''Arundo donax''). Invasive Plant Sci. Manag. 3, 495-505.</ref> It is reported that sterility of giant reed results from failure of the [[megaspore]] mother cell to divide.<ref>Bhanwra R.K., Choda S.P., Kumar S. 1982. Comparative embryology of some grasses. Proceedings of the Indian National Science Academy, 48, 152–162.</ref> This [[sterility (physiology)|sterility]], which drastically limits genetic variability, is an obstacle for breeding programs which aim to increase the productivity and [[biomass]] quality for energy conversion.<ref>Mariani C., R. Cabrini, A. Danin, P. Piffanelli, A. Fricano, S. Gomarasca, M. Dicandilo, F. Grassi and C. Soave. 2010 Origin, diffusion and reproduction of the giant reed (''Arundo donax'' L.) a promising weedy energy crop. Annals of Applied Biology. 157: 191–202.</ref>
A total of 185 clones of ''A. donax'' were collected from [[California]] to [[South Carolina]] and genetically fingerprinted with the [[sequence-related amplified polymorphism|SRAP]] and [[transposable element|TE]]-based markers.<ref>Ahmad R., Liow P.S., Spencer D.F., Jasieniuk M. 2008. [https://web.archive.org/web/20171209100255/https://naldc.nal.usda.gov/download/32160/PDF Molecular evidence for a single genetic clone of invasive ''Arundo donax'' in the United States]. Aquatic Botany. 88: 113–120.</ref> Giant reed exhibited no molecular genetic variation despite the wide [[genomic]] coverage of the markers used in this study. The molecular data strongly point to a single genetic clone of ''A. donax'' in the [[United States]], although multiple introductions of this plant into the [[United States]] have been documented. Another study conducted in the [[Mediterranean area]] sampled giant reed from 80 different sites, and demonstrated low gene diversity in this region as well. Results indicate the occurrence of post-[[meiotic]] alterations in the ovule and pollen developmental pathway. [[Amplified fragment length polymorphism|AFLP]] data support a [[monophyletic]] origin of giant reed and suggest that it originated in [[Asia]], spreading from there into the [[Mediterranean Basin]].

==Ecology==
Giant reed is adapted to a wide variety of ecological conditions, but is generally associated with riparian and wetland systems. It is distributed across the southern [[United States]] from [[Maryland]] to [[California]]. Plants can grow in a variety of soils, from heavy clays to loose sands and gravelly soils, but prefer wet drained soils, where they produce dense [[monotypic]] stands.

===Invasiveness and management===
Arundo is a highly invasive plant in southwestern North American rivers, and its promotion as a [[biofuel]] in other regions is of great concern to environmental scientists and land managers.<ref>Lambert, A.M., Dudley, T.L., Saltonstall, K., 2010. Ecology and impacts of the large-statured invasive grasses ''Arundo donax'' and ''Phragmites australis'' in North America. Invasive Plant Sci. Manag. 3, 489-494.</ref> ''Arundo donax'' was introduced from the Mediterranean to [[California]] in the 1820s for roofing material and erosion control in drainage canals in the Los Angeles area.<ref name=":3">{{Cite book |last=Bell |first=Gary P. |url=http://worldcat.org/oclc/44494430 |title=Ecology and management of Arundo donax and approaches to riparian habitat restoration in southern California |date=c. 1997 |publisher=[California Resources Agency] |oclc=44494430}}</ref><ref name=":1" /> Through spread and subsequent plantings as an [[ornamental plant]], and for use as reeds in woodwind instruments, it has become naturalised throughout warm coastal freshwaters of [[North America]], and its range continues to spread.

It has also been planted widely through [[South America]] and [[Australasia]]<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":2" /> and in [[New Zealand]] it is listed under the [[National Pest Plant Accord]] as an "unwanted organism".<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.biosecurity.govt.nz/pests/giant-reed|title=Giant reed|publisher=Biosecurity New Zealand|access-date=2009-01-13}}</ref> Despite its invasive characteristics in regions around the world where it is not native, Arundo is being promoted by the energy industry as a bio-fuel crop. Some of the regions, such as the southeastern United States have natural disturbances, such as hurricanes and floods, that could widely disperse this plant.

It is among the fastest-growing terrestrial plants in the world (nearly {{convert|10|cm}} per day).<ref name=":0" /> To present knowledge, Arundo does not provide any food sources or nesting habitats for wildlife. Replacement of native plant communities by Arundo results in low-quality habitat and altered ecosystem functioning.<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":1" /> For example, it damages California's riparian ecosystems by outcompeting native species, such as willows, for water. ''A. donax'' stems and leaves contain a variety of harmful chemicals, including silica and various [[alkaloids]], which protect it from most insect [[herbivores]] and deter wildlife from feeding on it.<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":4">{{Cite journal |last=Miles |first=D.Howard |last2=Tunsuwan |first2=Kwanjai |last3=Chittawong |first3=Vallapa |last4=Kokpol |first4=Udom |last5=Choudhary |first5=M.Iqbal |last6=Clardy |first6=Jon |date=November 1993 |title=Boll weevil antifeedants from Arundo donax |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/0031-9422(91)80015-s |journal=Phytochemistry |volume=34 |issue=5 |pages=1277–1279 |doi=10.1016/0031-9422(91)80015-s |issn=0031-9422|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name=":1" /> Grazing animals such as [[cattle]], [[sheep]], and [[goat]]s may have some effect on it, but are unlikely to be useful in keeping it under control.<ref name=":0" />

''Arundo donax'' appears to be highly adapted to fires. It is highly flammable throughout the year, and during the drier months of the year (July to October), it can increase the probability, intensity, and spread of wildfires through the riparian environment, changing the communities from flood-defined to fire-defined communities.<ref>Coffman, G., Ambrose, R., Rundel, P., 2010. Wildfire promotes dominance of invasive giant reed (''Arundo donax'') in riparian ecosystems. Biol. Invasions 12, 2723-2734.</ref> After fires, ''A. donax'' rhizomes can resprout quickly, outgrowing native plants, which can result in large stands of ''A. donax'' along riparian corridors.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Arundo Donax Workshop |url=http://worldcat.org/oclc/44509994 |title=Arundo Donax Workshop proceedings : November 19, 1993 |date=c. 1994 |publisher=Berkeley Digital Library Project |oclc=44509994}}</ref><ref name=":3" /> Fire events thus push the system further toward mono-specific stands of ''A. donax''.

A waterside plant community dominated by ''A. donax'' may also have reduced canopy shading of the in-stream habitat, which may result in increased water temperatures. This may lead to decreased oxygen concentrations and lower diversity of aquatic animals.<ref name=":3" />

As the impact of ''Arundo donax'' increased in the environment and native species various efforts have been taken to reduce its population. It has few natural enemies in its introduced range. Several Mediterranean insects have been imported into the United States as [[biological control]] agents.<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":4" /><ref name=":1" /> The Arundo wasp, ''[[Tetramesa romana]]'', the Arundo scale insect, ''[[Rhizaspidiotus donacis]]'', and the Arundo fly, ''[[Cryptonevra]]'' are known to have some effect in damaging the plant. ''Tetramesa romana'' and more recently ''Rhizaspidiotus donacisis'' were registered in the US as biological control agents.

Other remedies like using mechanical force have also been employed, since outside its native range ''Arundo donax'' does not reproduce by seeds, so removing its root structure can be effective at controlling it. Preventing it from getting sunlight will deplete the plant of its resources and eventually kill it.<ref name=":1" /> Systemic herbicides and [[glyphosate]] are also used as chemical remedies.

The US Department of Homeland Security considers this plant invasive and in 2007 began researching biological controls.<ref>{{Cite web | url=https://www.dhs.gov/science-and-technology/razing-cane | title=Razing Cane| date=2009-07-07}}</ref> In 2015, Texas Senator [[Carlos Uresti]] passed legislation to create a program to eradicate ''Arundo donax'' using herbicides and the Arundo wasp.<ref>{{cite news| url=https://www.texastribune.org/2016/04/05/new-carrizo-eradication-effort-reignites-old-debat/ | work=Texas Tribune | first=Julian | last=Aguilar | title=New Carrizo Eradication Effort Reignites Old Debate | date=2016-04-05}}</ref>

In [[New Zealand]]'s [[Northland Region|northernmost region]], ''Arundo donax'' crowds out native plants,<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/blogs-news-from-elsewhere-38680113|title=New Zealand imports insects to fight plant invader|date=2017-01-19|newspaper=BBC News|language=en-GB|access-date=2017-01-21}}</ref> reduces wildlife habitat, contributes to higher fire frequency and intensity, and modifies river hydrology.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=McAllister |title=Ecological impact of invasive ''Arundo donax'' populations in New Zealand: a 10 year study |journal=Journal of Ecology |date=2011 |volume=53 |issue=9 |pages=62–67}}</ref>

==Uses==

===Energy crop===
[[Energy crops]] are plants which are produced with the express purpose of using their biomass energetically<ref>Lewandowski I, Scurlock JMO, Lindvall E, Christou M. 2003. The development and current status of perennial rhizomatous grasses as energy crops in the US and Europe. Biomass and Bioenergy. 25:335–61.</ref> and at the same time reduce [[Greenhouse gas emissions|carbon dioxide emission]]. Biofuels derived from lignocellulosic plant material represent an important renewable energy alternative to transportation fossil fuels.<ref>Sanderson K. 2006. US biofuels: A field in ferment. Nature 444: 673-676.</ref> [[Perennial plant|Perennial]] [[rhizomatous]] [[grasses]] display several positive attributes as [[energy crops]] because of their high productivity, low (no) demand for [[nutrient]] [[Agricultural productivity|inputs]] consequent to the recycling of nutrients by their [[rhizomes]], exceptional soil [[carbon sequestration]] (4 times more than [[switchgrass]]), multiple products, adaptation to [[saline soils]] and [[saline water]], and resistance to [[biotic stress|biotic]] and [[abiotic stress]]es.

Giant reed is one of the most promising [[crops]] for [[energy production]] in the [[Mediterranean climate]] of Europe and Africa, where it has shown advantages as an [[Native plant|indigenous crop]] (already adapted to the [[natural environment|environment]]), durable [[crop yield|yields]], and resistant to long [[drought]] periods. Several field studies have highlighted the beneficial effect of giant reed crop on the environment due to its minimal soil [[tillage]], [[fertilizer]] and [[pesticide]] needs. Furthermore, it offers protection against [[soil erosion]],<ref>Heaton, E., Voigt, T., and Long, S.P. 2004. A quantitative review comparing the yields of two candidate C<sub>4</sub> perennial biomass crops in relation to nitrogen, temperature and water. Biomass and Bioenergy. 27:21–30.</ref> one of the most important [[land degradation]] processes in [[Mediterranean]] and [[United States|US]] environments. ''A. donax'' bioenergy feedstock has an impressive potential for several conversion processes. Dried biomass has a direct combustion high heating value of {{convert|8000|BTU/lb|kJ/kg|abbr=on|disp=flip}}.
In [[Italy]], ''Arundo donax'' was used in one instance from 1937 to 1962 on a large-scale industrial basis for paper and [[dissolving pulp]]. This interest was stimulated primarily by the desire of the [[Benito Mussolini|Mussolini]] dictatorship, just before [[World War II]], to be independent of foreign sources of [[textile]] fibres and the desire for an export product.<ref name="doi.org" /> According to historical records made by [[SNIA S.p.A.|Snia Viscosa]], giant reed was established on 6 300 [[Hectare|ha]] in [[Torviscosa]] ([[Province of Udine|Udine]]), reaching the average annual production of 35 [[ton|t]]/[[Hectare|ha]].<ref>Facchini 1941 La canna gentile per la Produzione Della cellulose mobile. L'impresa agricolo-Industriale di Torviscosa</ref> Today several screening studies on [[energy crops]] have been carried out by several universities in [[the United States|the US]] as well as in [[European Union|EU]] to evaluate and identify best management practices for maximizing biomass [[crop yield|yields]] and assess environmental impacts.

===Cultivation===
Establishment is a critical point of cultivation. The [[Plant stem|Stem]] and [[rhizome]] have a great ability to sprout after removal from mother plant and both can be used for [[Vegetative reproduction|clonal propagation]]. The use of [[rhizomes]] was found to be the better propagation method for this species, achieving better survival rate.<ref>Christou M, Mardikis M, Alexopoulou E. 2000. Propagation material and plant density effects on the ''Arundo donax'' yields. In: Biomass for energy and industry: proceeding of the First World Conference, Sevilla, Spain, June 5–9, 2000. p. 1622–8.</ref> In this field study, it was noticed how the lowest density (12,500 [[rhizomes]]/[[Hectare|ha]]) resulted in taller and thicker plants compared to denser [[plantation]] (25,000 [[rhizomes]]/[[Hectare|ha]]). [[Seedbed]] preparation is conducted in the [[Spring (season)|spring]], immediately before planting, by a pass with a double-disk harrowing and a pass with a [[field cultivator]]. Giant reed has the possibility of adopting low plant density. The [[rhizomes]] were planted at {{convert|10|–|20|cm}} of soil depth, with a minimum plant density of 10,000 plants per [[Hectare|ha]]), while mature [[Plant stem|stems]], with two or more nodes, can be planted {{convert|10|–|15|cm}} deep. In order to ensure good [[root]] stand and adequate contact with the [[soil]], sufficient moisture is needed immediately after planting. Pre-plant [[fertilizer]] is distributed according to the initial [[soil fertility]], but usually an application of [[Phosphorus|P]] at a rate of {{convert|80|–|100|kg}}/[[Hectare|ha]] is applied.

''A. donax'' maintains a high productive aptitude without [[irrigation]] under [[semi-arid climate]] conditions. In [[Southern Italy]], a trial was carried out testing the [[crop yield|yields]] performance of 39 [[genotype]]s, and an average [[crop yield|yields]] of 22.1 t/[[Hectare|ha]] dry matter in the second year were reached,<ref>Cosentino et al. 2006 First results on evaluation of ''Arundo donax'' (L.) clones collected in Southern Italy</ref> a comparable result with others results obtained in [[Spain]] (22.5 t/[[Hectare|ha]]) as well as in South [[Greece]] (19.0 t/[[Hectare|ha]]). Several reports underlined that it is more economical to grow giant reed under moderate [[irrigation]].

In order to evaluate different management practices, [[nitrogen]] [[fertilizer]] and [[Agricultural productivity|input]] demand was evaluated in a 6-year field study conducted at the [[University of Pisa]]. [[Fertilizer]] enhanced the productive capacity in the initial years, but as the years go by and as the radical apparatus progressively deepens, the differences due to fertilizer decrease until disappearing. [[Harvest]] time and plant density were found to not affect the biomass [[crop yield|yields]].

Due to its high growth rate and superior resource-capture capacity (light, water and nutrients), ''A. donax'' is not affected by weed competition from the second year. An application of post-emergence treatment is usually recommended.
Giant reed has few known [[Plant pathology|diseases]] or [[insect pest]]s, but in intensive cultivation, no pesticides are used.

To remove giant reed at the end of the crop cycle, there are mainly two methods: mechanical or chemical.<ref>Jackson 1998, Chemical control of giant reed (''Arundo donax'') and salt cedar (Tamarix ramosissima).</ref> An excavator can be useful to dig out the rhizomes or alternatively a single late-season application of 3% glyphosate onto the foliar mass is efficient and effective with least hazardous to biota.<ref>Spencer, D.F., Tan, W., Liow, P., Ksander, G., Whitehand, L.C., Weaver, S., Olson, J., Newhauser, M., 2008. Evaluation of glyphosate for managing giant reed (''Arundo donax''). InvasivePlantSci.Manage.1,248–254.</ref> Glyphosate was selected as the most appropriate product for specific considerations on efficacy, environmental safety, soil residual activity, operator safety, application timing, and cost-effectiveness. However, glyphosate is only effective in fall when plants are actively transporting nutrients to the root zone, and multiple retreatments are usually needed. Other herbicides registered for aquatic use can be very effective in controlling Arundo at other times of the year.

===Biofuel===
''Arundo donax'' is a strong candidate for use as a renewable biofuel source because of its fast growth rate and its ability to grow in different soil types and climatic conditions. ''A. donax'' will produce an average of three kilograms of biomass per square metre (12 tons per acre/year) once established.<ref name="Angelini, L.G. 2005, pp 375-389">Angelini, L.G., Ceccarinia, L., and Bonarib E.; European Journal of Agronomy, 22, 2005, pp 375-389</ref> The total energy input needed for the growing of one ha increases from not fertilised (4 GJ ha−1) to fertilised (18 GJ ha−1) crops, while the maximum energy yield output was 496 GJ ha−1, obtained with 20,000 plants per ha and fertilisation; fertilisation brought a 15% increase in biomass. The biomass calorific mean value (technically, the [[calorific value]] obtained from combustion of biomass sample in an adiabatic system) of Giant reed is about 17 MJ kg−1 dry matter regardless of fertilizer usage.<ref name="Angelini, L.G. 2005, pp 375-389" />

Studies in the European Union have identified ''A. donax'' as the most productive and lowest impact of all energy biomass crops (see FAIR REPORT E.U. 2004{{Citation needed|date=April 2025|reason=Why not actually link it?}}). Its ability to grow for 20 to 25 years without replanting is also significant. In the UK it is considered suitable for planting in and around water areas.<ref>BS 7370-5 Recommendations for maintenance of water areas</ref>

''Arundo donax'' grown in Australia was demonstrated as potential feedstock for producing advanced biofuels through [[hydrothermal liquefaction]].<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Kosinkova|first1=Jana|last2=Ramirez|first2=Jerome|last3=Jablonsky|first3=Michal|last4=Ristovski|first4=Zoran|last5=Brown|first5=Richard|last6=Rainey|first6=Thomas|title=Energy and chemical conversion of five Australian lignocellulosic feedstocks into bio-crude through liquefaction|journal=RSC Advances|date=24 May 2017|volume=7|issue=44|pages=27707–27717|doi=10.1039/C7RA02335A|bibcode=2017RSCAd...727707K|doi-access=free}}</ref>

Outside its native range, the interest as a biofuel crop needs to be balanced against its major invasive potential.

===Carbon sequestration===
An increased environmental concern is the health of soil system as one of the main factors affecting quality and productivity of agroecosystems. Around the world, several regions are subjected to a decline of fertility due to an increasing degradation of soils, loss of organic matter and increasing desertification.<ref>Albaladejo, J., and E. Díaz. 1990. Degradation and regeneration of the soil in a Mediterranean Spanish coastline: Trials in {{abbr|Lucdeme|Lucha contra la Desertificación en el Mediterráneo / Desertification Control in the Mediterranean Region}} project (Degradación y regeneración del suelo en el litoral mediterráneo español: Experiencias en el proyecto LUCDEME). In ''Soil degradation and rehabilitation in Mediterranean environmental conditions'' (''Degradación y regeneración del suelo en condiciones ambientales medíterráneas''), ed. J. Albaladejo et al., 191–214. Madrid: [[Spanish National Research Council|CSIC]].</ref> Recently research was carried out to evaluate, in the same pedological and climatic conditions, the impact of three long-term (14 years) agricultural systems, continuous giant reed, natural grassland, and cropping sequence, on the organic-matter characteristics and microbial biomass size in soil.<ref>Riffaldi, R., Saviozzi, A., Cardelli, A., Bulleri, F., and Angelini, L. 2010. Comparison of Soil Organic-Matter Characteristics under the Energy Crop Giant Reed, Cropping Sequence and Natural Grass. Communications in Soil Science and Plant Analysis, 41:173–180.</ref> The study pointed out that a long term Giant reed cropping system, characterized by low tillage intensity, positively affect the amount and quality of [[soil organic matter]]. ''Arundo donax'' showed greater values than tilled management system for total soil organic carbon, light fraction carbon, dissolved organic carbon, and microbial biomass carbon. Regarding the humification parameters, there were noticed any statistically differences between giant reed and a cropping sequence (cereals-legumes cultivated conventionally).

===Ethnobotany===
''Arundo donax'' has been cultivated throughout Asia, southern Europe, northern Africa, and the Middle East for thousands of years. [[Ancient Egypt]]ians wrapped their dead in the leaves. The canes contain [[silica]], perhaps the reason for their durability, and have been used to make [[fishing rod]]s and [[walking stick]]s.{{Citation needed|date=August 2010}} In [[Mauritius]], where ''Arundo'' is called "fatax", the stems are traditionally used to make [[broom]]s.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2004-05-25 |title=The art of making fatak brooms |url=https://lexpress.mu/s/article/art-making-fatak-brooms |access-date=2025-04-17 |website=lexpress.mu |language=fr}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Mauritius: Memories of the past - Marsan balye - The broom maker |url=https://mautourco.com/mauritius-memories-of-the-past-marsan-balye-the-broom-maker/ |access-date=2025-04-17 |website=Mautourco |language=en-GB}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2014-03-18 |title=Culture de fatak: Rs 300 la tonne proposées aux planteurs |url=https://lexpress.mu/s/article/culture-de-fatak-rs-300-la-tonne-proposees-aux-planteurs |access-date=2025-04-17 |website=lexpress.mu |language=fr}}</ref> Its stiff stems are also used as support for climbing plants or for [[vine]]s.{{Citation needed|date=August 2010}}

This plant may have been used in combination with [[harmal]] (''Peganum harmala'') to create a brew similar to the South American [[ayahuasca]], and may trace its roots to the [[Soma (drink)|Soma]] of [[folklore|lore]].<ref>S. Ghosal, S. K. Dutta, A. K. Sanyal, and Bhattacharya, "''Arundo donax'' L. (Gramineae), Phytochemical and Pharmacological Evaluation," in the Journal of Medical Chemistry, vol. 12 (1969), p. 480.</ref>

===Construction===
[[File:Roof construction with reeds - panoramio.jpg|thumb|Construction of a roof using reeds]]
Mature reeds are used in construction as raw material, given their excellent properties and tubular shape. Its resemblance to bamboo permits their combination in buildings, though ''Arundo'' is more flexible.

In rural regions of Spain, for centuries there has existed a technique named ''{{lang|es|cañizo}}'', consisting of rectangles of approximately 2 by 1 meters of woven reeds to which clay or plaster could be applied. A properly insulated ''{{lang|es|cañizo}}'' in a roof could keep its mechanical properties for over 60 years. Its high silicon content allows the cane to keep its qualities through time.
Its low weight, flexibility, good adherence of the ''{{lang|es|cañizo}}'' fabric and low price of the raw material have been the main reasons that this technique has been used. However, in the last decades, the rural migration from the countryside to urban centres and the extensive exploitation of land has reduced its use.

Recently, initiatives are being taken to recover the use of this material, combining ancient techniques from southern Iraq ''[[mudhif]]'' (reed houses) with new materials.

Diverse associations and collectives, such as CanyaViva, are pioneering in the research in combination with Spanish universities.

=== Musical instruments ===
[[File:Sets of free reed aerophone (free) - Soinuenea.jpg|thumb|Sets of free reed aerophones]]
Ancient Greeks used cane to make [[flute]]s, known as ''kalamaulos'', from ''kalamos'' ("cane") + ''aulos'' ("flute"). At the time, the best cane for flutes came from the banks of river [[Cephissus (Athenian plain)|Cephissus]], in [[Attica, Greece]]. Several ''kalamauloi'' tuned differently and tied together, made a ''[[syrinx]]''. Giant reed has been used to make [[flute]]s for over 5,000 years. The [[pan pipe]]s consist of ten or more pipes made from the cane. The ancient end-blown flute [[ney]] is made from the same reeds.<ref>{{Citation

===Other uses===
When young, ''A. donax'' is readily browsed by ruminants, but it becomes unpalatable when maturing.<ref>Heuzé V., Tran G., Giger-Reverdin S., Lebas F., 2015. Giant reed (''Arundo donax''). Feedipedia, a programme by INRA, CIRAD, AFZ and FAO. https://www.feedipedia.org/node/502 Last updated on December 7, 2015, 17:39</ref> ''A. donax'' has also been used in [[constructed wetland]]s for wastewater treatment.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Calheiros |first1=Cristina S.C. |last2=Quitério |first2=Paula V.B. |last3=Silva |first3=Gabriela |last4=Crispim |first4=Luís F.C. |last5=Brix |first5=Hans |last6=Moura |first6=Sandra C. |last7=Castro |first7=Paula M.L. |title=Use of constructed wetland systems with ''Arundo'' and ''Sarcocornia'' for polishing high salinity tannery wastewater |journal=Journal of Environmental Management |date=2012 |volume=95 |issue=1 |pages=66–71 |doi=10.1016/j.jenvman.2011.10.003 |pmid=22115512}}</ref>
